articleTitle: Engineers & electrons: A century of electrical progress
abstract: Spanning two centuries — with emphasis on the past 100 years-Engineers & Electrons is as much a revelation of the human side of engineering as it is a description of the technical accomplishments of the profession.

articleTitle: Judging by the cover: Most job interviewers make quick judgments about an applicant, based on appearance; judgments that can affect an entire interview and get you the job
abstract: Initially, you are what you wear, at least in the opinion of most people. In a few sweeping glances, assessments are made about your character, intelligence, and ability to succeed based on appearance. People will revise their opinion for better or worse as they get to know you at work. (Years may pass before some “higher-ups” get the chance. Future co-workers may never even get the chance if you show up in jeans at the interview.) So take time to consider the image you will project at interviews, and on the job.

articleTitle: A modern power system simulation laboratory: A power system engineering lab should be a priority for universities updating their facilities. One is currently being built at Virginia Tech
abstract: Electric power systems have been present in the curricula of most electrical engineering schools. Interest in this field has fluctuated over the years — presently many schools are reducing their offerings in electric power. However, a few institutions are attempting to not only keep the field of power engineering alive, but also to bring modern practices of electric power engineering into the classroom.

articleTitle: Accreditation: What it means to you: ABET's evaluations of engineering programs guarantee your educational investment by ensuring minimum levels of competence
abstract: Accreditation often seems to be a murky and confusing procedure, shrouded in mystery. In fact, it is a fairly straightforward process with formal and well-defined guidelines to ensure minimum acceptable levels of education.

articleTitle: On becoming an engineer part II: Staying power: Part II advises that you become a firmly anchored professional. Be a good technician, but don't become one. Above all, apply the engineering method
abstract: Once you have an engineering job, your lifetime task of remaining an engineer starts. In this second of three articles about your transition from the classroom to the “real world,” I suggest that you learn how to be a good technician, but that you carefully avoid actually becoming one, that you use the “engineering method,” and that you keep yourself well-equipped with good tools.

articleTitle: Genius, creativity and leadership: Studies indicate that creative productivity is the result of a combination of widely varying factors
abstract: Thomas Edison took out 1093 patents over his career, still the record at the U.S. Patent Office. No wonder, then, that he said genius was 99 percent perspiration and only 1 percent inspiration! And Edison's case can be considered fairly typical. A number of researchers have shown, in apply, so that the proportion of “hits” to “misses” tends to be about the same for contributors of different quantities of work. Those who produce more masterworks also produce more rubbish. Thus, the best approach is to massively generate ideas in the hope that some pan out. This, of course, is the notion underlying “brainstorming” and similar techniques.

articleTitle: Creative problem solving combining man and machine: Problem solving in the computer age must make use of the unique abilities of humans and machines
abstract: What kinds of tools for human imaginative thinking are most suitable for the era of computers? How can we prepare to be more creative and productive in professional work, and in dealing with personal, everyday-life situations? How can we creatively anticipate and act on change?

articleTitle: Speech applications created by a microcomputer: Discover the advantages of newly developed single-chip microcomputers for digital signal processing in speech applications
abstract: One of the most popular applications of digital signal processing is speech processing, wherein speech may be analyzed, compressed, coded, synthesized, or recognized. As recently as a few years ago, this type of signal processing was done with a system comprised of a minicomputer, an array processor, and a large storage system. Nowadays, with the advances made by the semiconductor industry, a speech processing system may be condensed into a large-scale integrated circuit.

articleTitle: EE at work: A job with diversity at Kodak: For Cynthia Bell, the multidisciplinary work at Kodak's research labs was the answer to her quest for a job with variety
abstract: When Cynthia Bell interviewed at Kodak's Rochester, N.Y., headquarters during her senior year in college, she found Kodak's Corporate Research Laboratories just right for her. “What I wanted was a company that could offer me variety, so I could sort out what I do best,” says the 25-year-old research scientist.

articleTitle: Ada: A new programming language: The Department of Defense developed an incredible new programming language and named it in honor of Ada Lovelace, the world's first programmer
abstract: Fortran and Pascal have long been used by engineers to solve problems. Now a new programming language called Ada is expected to become the language used by many engineers, especially those employed by companies who work for the U.S. Department of Defense (DOD).

articleTitle: An introduction to standard-cell VLSI design: Very large scale integration (VLSI) is becoming an important means of producing electronic circuits at low cost, on tight schedules, and with protection for proprietary designs
abstract: The advantages of VLSI are many, including lower parts count, smaller boards, nonreverse engineerable designs, and lower power. The disadvantages, however, include a certain amount of design inflexibility and a penalty for design miscalculations or design changes that result in a requirement for a larger than anticipated area of silicon on the IC chip.

articleTitle: The laser as tactical and strategic weapon: Laser technology has revolutionized conventional warfare and promises to transform dramatically the way battles are fought
abstract: In 1972, in Operation Linebacker, the Thanh-Hoa Bridge (Vietnam) was completely destroyed via a laser-designated bomb after repeated attempts with ordinary bombs failed to eliminate the bridge at a cost of more than 100 lost or damaged aircraft. Since then, the unique properties of laser technology have been exploited to provide the modern military force with combat capabilities that existed only in thought just a few years ago [Fig. 1]. Current and proposed laser devices will revolutionize the way in which battles are fought.

articleTitle: Marketing yourself for the perfect job: Hard work, talent, and a well-planned campaign will help you prepare yourself for a competitive job market
abstract: How do you go after the right job — and get it? When your great job suddenly doesn't seem so great anymore, and you decide it's time to move on, what do you do? What happens if your job is phased out?

articleTitle: EE and M.B.A.: A winning combination? Is the M.B.A. overrated, or is it essential for career fulfillment? A group of experts cautions you to look before you leap
abstract: Many engineers view the master's of business administration degree as a magical open sesame to management and the big money of high-tech industry. But before you succumb to the supposed enchantment of the M.B.A., you should look carefully beyond the fantasy.

articleTitle: Educational opportunities in telecommunications beckon EEs: A promising career in this high-growth field can begin with a university program that offers specialized training
abstract: The field of telecommunications promises to be one of the areas offering the hottest career opportunities in the next several years, and experts are predicting shortages of trained personnel. Engineers will be needed to design, build, and manage the communications networks and services needed by industrial companies, banks, credit card companies, and the military — to mention just a few of the major users.

articleTitle: EE at work: Building a multi-faceted engineering career: Dual-degree Davy Hwang has gone out of his way to explore the many aspects of engineering and manufacturing
abstract: Finally, after seven long years and over 200 credits, Davy T. Hwang was ready for the engineering world, with a B.S. degree in both Electrical Engineering and Industrial Engineering, with a Business minor.

articleTitle: Fitting in: A story revealing that words and electrons can mix: A wide variety of careers in engineering publishing are open to the EE graduate
abstract: Mark was troubled. It all had begun very early that morning when he was out for his daily run. Tom had joined him.

articleTitle: The burnout syndrome: Reducing the risks: As a young, talented, electrical engineer-to-be, you are a likely candidate for burnout. Here's how to avoid emotional and physical short-circuiting
abstract: Chris has always been aware of what she's wanted, has gone after it, and has been able to get it. She's from a family of high achievers; both her parents are successful lawyers and her older brother is a surgery resident. Chris fits the family mold. She was president of her high school class and the valedictorian. Now she's studying electrical engineering at a first-rate university. Last summer she landed a job with a leading electronics company and has continued on as a consultant while completing college. She's virtually guaranteed a great job upon graduation.

articleTitle: Robert A. Millikan: Father of modern physics: This Nobel Prize winner's investigations provided the impetus for the scientific changes that have taken place in this century
abstract: Robert Andrew Millikan's parents expected him to work hard and contribute to the church. The long-lasting influence of this work ethic, which he held throughout his life, led to his painstaking research on the nature of matter and enabled him to become a self-made scientist. In 1923 Millikan won the Nobel Prize for physics for his work on the measurement of the charge of the electron and for his work on the photoelectric effect. He was the second American physicist to be awarded a Nobel Prize. Often considered one of the harbingers of modern physical theory, Millikan contributed to modern physics as a teacher, author, researcher, administrator, entrepreneur, and public figure.

articleTitle: Underground phenomena imaging using electromagnetic geophysical tomography: Electromagnetic geophysical tomography is a new technique used to characterize prospective urban subways, locating tunnels and natural caverns, mapping fractures in rock, and in delineating groundwater pathways
abstract: Computerized axial tomography (CAT) has been successfully used in medical diagnostics for nearly a decade. Doctors routinely use CAT images to locate and evaluate tumors or other abnormalities in the head and abdomen of patients. In the mid-1970s, an adaptation of the CAT concept was developed at the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory to investigate rock below the ground surface [Fig. 1]. This geophysical exploration technique has been employed in a wide range of applications including characterizing a prospective urban transit station prior to excavation.

articleTitle: EE at work: Powerful short term job benefits: “Working the service end of a power company was something I wanted to do. A summer working at the American Electric Power Company helped me realize this”
abstract: Michael Oatts enjoys day to day, short term activity more than long term planning activities. While working in the summer for his fellowship, he did long term planning for the American Electric Power Company, and said he found it much more rewarding to work on daily projects that are not just hypothetical ideas that may or may not be of use 10 years down the road. He comments “sometimes you would put a lot of work and energy into long term project and get really excited about it, only to find out that minds have changed.”

articleTitle: Reading up books: Reference for design of fault tolerant systems: Learn how to design systems that are highly reliable, highly available, and easily maintainable
abstract: In a narrow sense, a fault tolerant system is one that is capable of error-free operation as seen from the terminals of the system, even though some internal components may have failed. Thus, the use of backup computers on a space mission allows the safe return of the crew to Earth, even though the primary computer may have failed. The vehicle is said to be tolerant of faults in the primary computer system. This design technique, known as the standby spare technique, is a familiar example of the use of redundant components in the design of fault tolerant systems. There are a great many critical applications where human life depends on the proper operation of electronic equipment. Medical equipment, automatic landing systems on commercial aircraft, and nuclear reactor controllers are just a few of these life-critical systems. Such applications require extremely highly reliable designs.

articleTitle: Semiconductor lasers: A choice structure for lightwave communications
abstract: Since its first demonstration in the early 1960s, the semiconductor laser has become the center of a tremendously important communications technology — fiber-optic communications. In terms of structure, design, and operation, the semiconductor laser has much in common with all other forms of lasers. It has an active medium that provides optical amplification (gain) under the appropriate circumstances. This active medium is typically a compound semiconductor from the III-V family (combinations of elements from columns III and V of the periodic chart), such as gallium arsenide (GaAs). The III-Vs are direct energy gap semiconductors that, unlike the silicon used in integrated circuitry, are very efficient light emitters. The feedback cavity for semiconductor lasers is easily obtained by using the natural reflectivity of the parallel cleavage planes of these single-crystal materials. Finally, the semiconductor laser is very efficient and requires only a few volts at modest current levels (200 milliamperes).

articleTitle: Patent strategies for inventors: What's the use of getting a patent? Do they protect inventors, or is there some other purpose? What if something is invented but not patented?
abstract: You have seen it before: A newspaper article reports the hard luck case of an inventor with a great idea, patenting it, and making little or no money on the invention.

articleTitle: EE at work: At home in the lab with semiconductor lasers: A journey that began in the oil fields of Burma has brought this EE home to the lab researching and building “different kinds of lasers”
abstract: From Sweden to Burma to the Philippines to New Jersey — with a variety of stops along the way — electrical engineer Anders Olssen has traveled a long and winding road to reach his current position as an MTS (member of the technical staff), with AT&T Bell Laboratories in Murray Hill, N.J.

articleTitle: Keys to job selection success, or, how to keep the romance growing: In the spring, the old saying goes, a young man's fancies turn to love. But during the bleak days of late fall, the focus for rising engineering graduates (of each gender) is clearly the “wooing” of potential employers
abstract: Unlike the fancies of spring, a successful job search must be an affair of the head, not of the heart. Every expectant graduate hopes for a job/career romance that will last well past the early honeymoon in the first job as an engineering professional. This is the time for clear thinking, careful planning and deliberate decision-making to avoid the job market seductions of cleverly orchestrated interviews, well-rehearsed interviewers, exciting locations, and enticing job titles and salaries. The key to job selection consists of putting the passion of the job search moment aside and concentrating on the “morning after” realities of the engineering positions being offered.

articleTitle: Lasers: The healing tool of the future: Fulfillment of their far-reaching potential depends on the work of physicians and engineers to understand laser-tissue interactions and develop new technologies
abstract: Scientists predict that lasers will revolutionize the practice of medicine and surgery. Whether this proves to be true will depend on the success of current and future research. Few, if any, laser-tissue interactions (the backbone of laser medicine) are completely understood, although lasers have been used in medicine since 1961. The physical and biological response to laser irradiation is complex and occurs on spatial and temporal scales that are difficult to study. On the other hand, progress in this field also strongly depends on advances in basic laser technology, which provide the tools of the trade. Thus, the field of lasers in medicine is ripe for the innovative work of engineers, basic scientists, and physicians.

articleTitle: Campus interviews — “What do they want from me?” Approach on-campus interviews by considering what is right for you
abstract: I have occasion to speak to student groups fairly frequently in my role as Regional Recruiting Manager for General Electric. To get job-hunting students on the right track, I tell them that, instead of asking “What is the company interviewer looking for in me?” they might better approach the interview cycle with this question: “How can I select the job opportunity that's right and the company that's best for me?”

articleTitle: Alternate power production technologies: The promise and the challenge: Near-term and long-term generation alternatives can contribute to our energy resource base, but technological and environmental problems remain
abstract: Since the oil embargo of 1973, the top research priority of most electric utility companies has been on how best to use alternate power generation technologies and replace oil-fired generation with clean and abundant domestic sources of energy. The technologies considered fall into two broad categories, near-term alternatives and long-term renewables, each posing unique problems and solutions.

articleTitle: On becoming an engineer part III: Civic responsibility: Even at the pinnacle of your career, your task is not done. New challenges await you as a citizen engineer
abstract: Everybody uses the products of engineering. The most ardent antitechnologists read printing, ride in vehicles, wear eyeglasses, wear running shoes, drink liquids, or occasionally determine the time. The typical citizen readily accepts automatic transmission, television sets, portable cassette players, processed food, readily available energy and communications systems, and other technical artifacts of our civilization. On the extreme end of the scale, there are those who almost compulsively have to go out and buy the latest gadget or gizmo. As engineers, we are the principal source for these developments that affect so many people. As such, we have some additional obligations as citizen engineers. In this final article about your transition from the classroom to the “real world,” I comment on our unique perspective as engineers and on our responsibility to communicate our insights to those in our society who lack technical training and understanding.

articleTitle: Trigonometric identities using frequency domain techniques: With practice, it is easier to derive most trigonometric identities than it is to look them up
abstract: The engineer is always learning procedures and techniques that make the solving of certain types of problems easier. These techniques often use simplification procedures that not only simplify the analysis, but also transform the problem so that it can be solved using familiar techniques. A good example of this is the solution of electrical circuits where the sources are sinusoidal. The set of integral-differential equations describing the circuit is transformed into a set of simultaneous algebraic equations involving complex numbers. The writing and solving of these equations deal with techniques that are already a familiar part of the engineer's bag-of-tricks. The circuit is transformed into what is called the “frequency domain,” and the emphasis is transformed into one of learning how to deal with complex numbers and complex functions.

articleTitle: Personal financial planning: Develop a good financial plan for yourself at an early age and assure a secure future
abstract: Suppose a friend told you that he had made a 10 percent return on his investments in 1984. Is that good? Bad? Should you congratulate him or laugh at him? It all depends on what his goals were and how much risk he was willing to take. Compared to the inflation rate of 4 percent in 1984 he did well. Compared to one measure of stock market performance, the S&P 500 Index, which was up 6.3 percent, he did well. Compared to long-term government bonds, up 15.5 percent, he did poorly. Maybe his expectation was just to keep up with inflation; maybe he took an enormous risk hoping to make a big killing. Your response depends on his investment goals.

articleTitle: Be safe, not sorry, when dealing with electricity: Conscientious attention to proper safety measures should become completely ingrained — Don't take unnecessary chances with your life
abstract: Electricity is a powerful force that can be dangerous if safety precautions are not followed. Although we use electricity every day, we must treat it with proper understanding and respect to avoid injury, and even death.

articleTitle: Electric power systems: The computer connection: Applications — Ranging from billing to payroll to system planning, design, and operation — Make the power industry the third largest user of computers
abstract: Many people believe that the only connection between power systems and computers is that computers must be plugged into an electrical outlet to operate. True, electricity does indeed power computers, either directly for desktop units or indirectly through uninterruptible power supplies (batteries charged by the power system) for large computers. There is far more, however, to the connection between computers and power systems.
“In the true modern spirit, the students were expected to create new knowledge not just learn things already known.” The Human side of Engineering: Tales of General Electric Engineering over 80 years

articleTitle: Computer-aided control system design at Cornell: Student reaction is positive to the incorporation of emerging computer-aided control system design (CACSD) software in the teaching of introductory control systems theory in the School of Electrical Engineering at Cornell University
abstract: A popular course in most electrical engineering curricula is control systems theory. It is one of the prominent extensions of the theoretical core of network theory. At most universities the emphasis in control systems theory courses is on computationally intensive analysis and design, which are at the heart of control engineering. Over the last few years, an increasing number of university and industrial researchers have been exploiting the power of the computer to perform such sequences of computation and data display needed in control system design. These computer aids in the control system design and simulation process have allowed these engineers to focus their efforts more substantially on the complex decisions needed in the selection of an appropriate controller.
“To my dismay, I watched one hearer after another silently rise, edge to the door, and disappear. I began to fear that I would have no hearers left.”

articleTitle: Job fit and creativity: “Our great mistake is to neglect the cultivation of those virtues that a person has … to try to exact from each person virtues he does not possess
abstract: He may not have known it at the time, but Hadrian was probably one of the first career counselors and we are still struggling to fully understand and apply his advice regarding job fit. Most acknowledge that it is important to understand who we are before we look at who we should be. And most will agree that there is mutual benefit to employees and organizations when there is a good match between the employee and the job. But economic and business pressures are powerful and “square pegs” often end up in “round holes” to meet the needs of individuals and organizations.

articleTitle: A sensible approach to teaching mathematics: In many math courses, such as calculus, the majority are engineering students but the instructors, consciously or unconsciously, present the subject as if they were planning a career in pure mathematics
abstract: We teach Mathematics at a Big Ten school with a large and selective engineering college. In the beginning of our careers, we too stated careful definitions and proved theorems, but found that our formal mathematical language which was intended to prevent misunderstanding had precisely the opposite effect. It obscured ideas that students would otherwise find straightforward. For example the formalism

articleTitle: Student papers contest: Writing a good technical paper can get you a job and provide beneficial background for the future
abstract: I see you've written a technical paper — tell me about it.” All of a sudden the tension eased for the new graduate engineer as he interviewed for his first professional job. He really wanted this job — and so did a hundred other applicants. It was with a prestigious employer, paid well, and offered opportunities for growth and advancement in precisely the field of his interests. He had the courses and grades to be competitive, but the interviewer appeared to be more interested in his student paper! — the work that had placed third in the IEEE Student Paper Contest. The interviewer knew well the value of engineers in her company who could communicate effectively. She, a senior engineer, was impressed with the initiative of this student and the way he could clearly express the essence of his paper, explain the technical problems, how he solved them, and how he related interesting findings with the well chosen graphical representations that he sketched while talking. His enthusiasm and ability to inform on a technical topic in a few minutes of the interview gave him an overwhelming edge over the other candidates.

articleTitle: View from the top: Laser technology: Its evolution into the marketplace: The search for coherent radiation at higher frequencies has spawned a lucrative commercial and military world market
abstract: Use of the electromagnetic spectrum has always been marked by a steady drive toward the production and application of coherent electromagnetic energy of higher and higher frequencies. Much of the impetus for this research comes from the realization that increasing carrier frequency has a positive impact on the amount of transmitted information, on directivity, and on efficiency, and alleviates problems of crowding and interference between existing frequency bands. Another important reason is research interest in using these waves for probing atoms in solids, liquids, and gases by employing experimental techniques such as nuclear magnetic resonance, paramagnetic resonance, and cyclotron resonance.

“We have for two years past been making use of the electric light, and our experience with it makes its use on a larger scale very desirable. Its safety, steadiness, agreeableness to the eye, its economy, and last, but not least — its educating power, have been fully demonstrated here, and I hope that we may secure the means necessary for a permanent use of the system. The cost, as nearly as we can now estimate, will be reduced by special terms, to $6000.”

articleTitle: Resume writing: A solid resume is the first step toward getting the job of your dreams
abstract: Job wanted: Exciting, well-paying position. … The dream job you envision while sitting through those boring classes. Depending on how realistic your dreams are, that job might be out there, or at least a reasonable facsimile of it. The only catch is making yourself the ‘dream person’ for that position. And that is where your resume, which summarizes you and why you are the person the company wants, comes in.

articleTitle: Reading up books: An introduction to laser literature: Laser technology will produce new discoveries and new challenges, providing fertile ground for the well-trained and the well-read
abstract: Lasers and electro-optics are two of the most exciting fields that a new graduate can consider. Much of this excitement comes from the challenge of working to produce new coherent wavelengths from known materials. Added incentive comes from using these new wavelengths to do things that have never been done before, such as rejoining a detached retina without an incision or helping to manufacture electronic chips with more components per unit area than ever before.

articleTitle: View from the top: The ever-expanding domain of electronic technology: Today's EE must be ever-ready to serve our dynamic society
abstract: What is happening in technology is not exactly clear, and as we view the future we can see significant change and advancement, with the exact impact of these changes not yet clearly visible.

articleTitle: Laser technology: Theory and operating principles: Application of the principles of quantum electronics has yielded hundreds of lasers whose wavelengths span from the infrared to the X-ray region of the spectrum
abstract: This month marks the 25th anniversary of the discovery of the laser. In the quarter century since Theodore H. Maiman first produced a beam of deep red light from a ruby rod, intensive research has yielded literally hundreds of lasers whose wavelengths now span the electromagnetic spectrum from the infrared region to the threshold of the X-ray region. The impact of lasers and of quantum electronics — the area to which the laser gave impetus — on scientific research is best attested to by the six Nobel laureates that the field has produced. However, the laser is no longer the sole domain of the physicist or the chemist, but has moved in a dramatic way into the factory, the hospital, and the home. This is reflected by the rapidly expanding laser market. Since the 1962 introduction of the first commercial laser, the sales of lasers and laser systems have grown steadily, peaking at 1984's record level of $4.4 billion, according to Laser Focus magazine's annual market survey. This article presents a brief overview of the theory and operation of the laser and discusses several of its most prominent applications. In-depth coverage of selected topics is presented in accompanying articles.

articleTitle: Commercial/industrial lasers in a demanding environment: In the commercial/industrial environment, lasers are a unique source of power for tasks ranging from materials processing to printing to optical recording
abstract: It is hard even for “old hands” to recognize that practical lasers have been around for a quarter century. At first, these new kinds of light sources, with their remarkably increased light generation capabilities, were used in the laboratory, where scientists traditionally turn quickly to each new tool that can open up additional ways of looking at the physical world. Engineering applications developed much more slowly.

articleTitle: View from the top: Preparing for the future: Electrical engineering graduates are expected to be prepared for a career in what is perhaps the fastest changing area of technology — Prepare now for technologies that haven't yet been invented!
abstract: As the IEEE closed its Centennial year, we looked back at the century of giants who have shown us the way to become prepared for a career of change. The first President of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers (one of the two predecessor founder organizations of the IEEE) was Norvin Green. Mr. Green was also the President of Western Union Telegraph Company, which was viewed by many as the foremost “high-tech” company of that day. Also, on the executive committee of the AIEE in 1884 were two people called Edison and Bell. Most of us recognize the names, Edison and Bell, but we hardly know what a telegraph was, much less remember Norvin Green.

Twenty-five years have passed since Theodore H. Maiman first demonstrated laser action in a ruby crystal. In transcending the microwave region of the spectrum, Maiman's accomplishment left wide open for exploration the infrared, visible, and ultraviolet regions.
